question: Assume today is 2026-08-29. You know nothing published after this date. Estimate the total freight carried by Canadian railways in July 2026, in tonnes, as it will be first reported by Statistics Canada in its monthly Railway carloadings release (total traffic carried, Canada).

target.what: Total freight carried by Canadian railways (all traffic carried, Canada) during July 2026, as first reported by Statistics Canada in its monthly Railway carloadings release (Table 23-10-0079-01 / The Daily release). Counts all revenue freight loaded and carried by Canadian Class I and regional railw
target.caveats: Working interpretation: 'total traffic carried' = total freight tonnage originated/loaded by Canadian railways in the month (the headline 'total traffic carried' figure in the Railway carloadings release), not tonnage-km and not just domestic traffic. Alternative interpretations: (a) total tonnage i

candidates.hypothesis: July tonnage follows a stable seasonal pattern relative to adjacent months and prior Julys; the July 2026 value can be anchored on July 2023-2025 reported totals plus recent monthly levels, adjusted for trend. Role: provides the base level and seasonal shape.
candidates.data_to_find: Statistics Canada Table 23-10-0079-01 monthly total traffic carried (tonnes), Canada, all months 2023-01 through the latest month published before 2026-08-29 (likely June 2026); also the July values for 2023, 2024, 2025 and the June/July month-over-month ratios.

assumptions.name: July 2026 year-over-year growth factor for Canadian rail tonnage
assumptions.rationale: Cumulative Canadian carloads+intermodal through week 28 of 2026 are up 0.6% year over year (p51/p52), while weekly July 2026 carloads are up 1.9-3.8% and intermodal down 1.4-3.2% (p47-p50, p56-p59). A near-flat to slightly positive growth factor centered on +0.6% with a range spanning the mixed weekly signals is the best transfer from carload counts to tonnage.
assumptions.applies_when: The July 2026 tonnage tracks the same year-over-year direction as Canadian carload+intermodal counts; tonnage per carload is roughly stable.
assumptions.falsified_by: Evidence that July 2026 tonnage per carload shifted materially (e.g., a commodity mix shift toward heavy bulk) or a disruption in late July 2026.

assumptions.name: July 2026 year-over-year growth factor from US rail traffic
assumptions.rationale: US rail traffic in July 2026 is up ~1.5-3.4% year over year (p42, p63), with carloads down ~0.4-1.2% and intermodal up 3-7.2%. Canadian traffic is correlated but not identical; a modest positive factor near +2% is a reasonable transfer.
assumptions.applies_when: Canadian and US rail volumes move together in July 2026 as they historically have.
assumptions.falsified_by: Evidence of divergence between Canadian and US rail volumes in July 2026 (e.g., a Canada-specific disruption or commodity shock).

methods.label: m1

p1.role: Total cargo carried by Canadian railways, all traffic, Canada, July 2025 (tonnes)

a1.role: Year-over-year growth factor for July 2026 vs July 2025 Canadian rail tonnage

methods.rationale: Anchors on the July 2025 StatCan total (p1) and scales by the cumulative 2026 Canadian carload/intermodal growth (+0.6%, p52) as a volume-growth proxy. Shared dependency: p1 and the growth signal both come from rail volume data; failure mode is that tonnage growth diverges from carload growth due to commodity mix.

methods.label: m2

p1.role: Total cargo carried by Canadian railways, all traffic, Canada, July 2025 (tonnes)

a2.role: Year-over-year growth factor for July 2026 vs July 2025 Canadian rail tonnage, transferred from US rail traffic growth

methods.rationale: Anchors on p1 and scales by a US-rail-traffic-derived growth factor (p54, p42, p63). Transfer assumption: US growth proxies Canadian growth; Canadian traffic grew more slowly in 2026, so the factor is centered below US growth. Failure mode: decoupling of Canadian and US rail volumes.

methods.label: m3
methods.rationale: Naive carry-forward of the most recent July total (July 2025, p1 = 30.7 Mt), with July 2024 (p80) providing a second year for backtesting. Assumes July 2026 is close to July 2025; ignores the modest 2026 growth signal, so it serves as a stable baseline.

kept.name: July 2026 year-over-year growth factor for Canadian rail tonnage
kept.rationale: Canadian cumulative carloads+intermodal through week 28 of 2026 are +0.6% (p52), and recent weeks are mixed (carloads up, intermodal down). Tonnage growth is assumed to track this modest volume growth, centered at +0.6% with a range reflecting commodity-mix and intermodal weakness.
kept.applies_when: July 2026 Canadian rail tonnage grows roughly in line with cumulative 2026 carload/intermodal volume growth.
kept.falsified_by: Evidence that July 2026 tonnage diverged sharply from the +0.6% cumulative volume trend (e.g., a major disruption or commodity surge).

kept.name: July 2026 year-over-year growth factor transferred from US rail traffic
kept.rationale: US cumulative carloads+intermodal are +3.4% (p54) and recent weeks +1.5% to +3.4% (p42, p63); Canadian traffic historically correlates with US but grew more slowly (+0.6%), so the transfer is centered near +2% with a wide range.
kept.applies_when: US rail growth is a reasonable proxy for Canadian rail tonnage growth in July 2026.
kept.falsified_by: Evidence that Canadian and US rail traffic decoupled in mid-2026 (e.g., Canadian-specific disruptions or commodity divergence).

by_construction: Only URLs leave the searcher (code regex); extractor, judge and final prompts never contain search result titles, snippets or the searcher's text. This holds by construction and is not measured.
residual_risks: The searcher sees post-cutoff search results and chooses which URLs are fetched, so page selection can be conditioned on the answer; only the URLs leave the searcher, and in backtests every fetched page is a snapshot dated <= as_of.
Live pages are used only when as_of is today; in backtests every page is an archived snapshot dated <= as_of.
The leak sentinel only catches registered official values in common formats, not paraphrased or derived numbers.
The model's own training data (knowledge cutoff unpublished) can include history before as_of; it cannot include the target if the target was published after the model's release.
Wayback snapshots are captured by a third party; a snapshot date <= as_of proves the content existed by then.
Assumption values are proposed by the judge model from its own knowledge, which can include the target's history before as_of; code checks their form, not where the number came from.
